summary:
Rio Grande do Norte stands under Brazil's national framework. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change in 2018, the age of consent is equal regardless of sexual orientation, and since the Supreme Court's 2019 ruling constitutional and federal criminal provisions prohibit discrimination and hate crimes on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds, with transphobia punishable on the same footing as racism. An expat legal guide updated in April 2026 confirms that marriage recognition, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate across the country, so a trans visitor's status and documents are handled like anyone else's at entry and in family matters. No state-level statutory restriction or unique legal finding applies in Rio Grande do Norte.

The dominant visitor-facing signal is lethal violence against trans people. ANTRA's dossier for 2024 recorded 122 trans and travesti killings nationally, 16 per cent below the 145 recorded in 2023 and close to the 125-per-year average for 2008 to 2024; five of the victims were human-rights defenders and 95.9 per cent were travestis or trans women. The same dossier documents systematic under-counting because official bodies do not record LGBTQIA+ victims properly, which is the basis on which Rio Grande do Norte appeared with zero recorded killings in 2024.

The ninth ANTRA dossier, covering 2025, records 80 trans killings nationwide, Brazil's eighteenth consecutive year at the top of the global tally. In the state ranking Ceará and Minas Gerais lead with eight each, while Paraíba and Rio Grande do Norte appear with four each. Against a population of roughly 3.5 million, four cases yield about 1.14 killings per million per year, the highest per-capita rate among all 27 units in 2025 and around three times the national figure of roughly 0.38 per million. The jump from zero in 2024 makes Rio Grande do Norte the sharpest deterioration in the dataset, and the dataset itself cautions against reading a single-year zero as evidence of safety.

Lethal violence against trans women in the state continued after both counted years. In the early hours of 4 May 2026, Emanuelle Samira Fernandes Neta, a 27-year-old transgender woman, was shot dead inside her rented home in the Dom Jaime Câmara neighbourhood of Mossoró after five men broke in and killed her while she slept; military police found the body on a routine patrol and one suspect was arrested with a pistol and booked for illegal firearms discharge and armed criminal association. In late February 2026 a transgender woman known as Naomi was found dead in her own home in Praia da Pipa, in the Tibau do Sul municipality, killed by stab wounds, with the Civil Police opening an investigation.

Detention, if it arises, is governed by national rather than state rules. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, requires that a person held as LGBTI be recognised by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing, and that placement be fixed by a reasoned judicial decision after the person has been consulted about their preference. Trans, travesti and intersex people must be asked whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit and within it the general population or a specific wing or cell; LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited. No Rio Grande do Norte placement policy is documented in the sources held, and practice elsewhere in the country has been found to diverge sharply from this framework.
tangentialFactors:
The violence picture is regional as well as national. Of the 80 trans killings recorded in Brazil in 2025, 38 fell in the Northeast, the region containing Rio Grande do Norte, and the two states topping the ranking, Ceará and Minas Gerais, recorded eight each. Small absolute numbers mean a single incident moves a state's rate sharply, and the volatility between 2024 and 2025 indicates an environment that can turn quickly rather than one that has stabilised.

Official recording is unreliable in the victim's favour. ANTRA's 2024 dossier attributes the low national count partly to systematic under-counting by official bodies that do not record LGBTQIA+ victims properly, so a recorded figure of zero is a data artefact of the counting method as much as an assessment of risk.

Beyond the state, national conditions supply the background against which a trans visitor moves. In the October 2024 municipal elections close to 1,000 transgender candidates stood across every state of the country and received death threats and intimidation, while the number of trans officeholders tripled compared with the previous cycle. A May 2024 investigation documented drink-spiking robberies in which LGBTQIA+ people are targeted in São Paulo nightlife. Courts have also applied the hate-crime provisions to commercial conduct: the 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing.

The gap between protective text and practice is documented in detention. A peer-reviewed census carried out between April and June 2021 interviewed 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates inside eleven units treated as masculine in the Rio de Janeiro state prison system, finding trans women housed in units operated as masculine or in so-called neutral or security units, and describing placement in male units as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights. The same study records a 2015 Rio de Janeiro state law granting parity of treatment with cisgender women in women's units, covering hair length, clothing, accessories and cosmetics.

Protection machinery has widened nationally: an analysis of case law from 2022 records lower courts pressing the Superior Court of Justice toward unanimously extending the remedies of the Maria da Penha Law and the Feminicide Law to trans women.
localsOnly:
Residents held in custody in Rio Grande do Norte are governed by National Council of Justice Resolutions 348/2020 and 366/2021. A person is recognised as LGBTI for placement purposes by self-declaration before a judge, the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units must be set out and the person asked which they prefer, the declared preference is recorded, and a later change of placement is possible. Transfers are prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat, LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.

Prisoners in Brazil more generally have the right to be referred to by their social name rather than their birth name, may be forwarded to women's prisons, and may choose male or female clothing; LGBTQ prisoners are described as having a distinct place in the prison system separate from other prisoners.

State-level advocacy and follow-up after killings come from the trans-rights association ATTRANSPARÊNCIA/RN, which publicly mourned Emanuelle Samira Fernandes Neta as an artist killed by the transphobia she faced and called for justice in the Praia da Pipa case. Investigations are handled by the Civil Police, with the Military Police discovering the Mossoró body on patrol.

Document and family matters, including legal gender change and marriage recognition, follow national rules administered without a surgical requirement, so a resident's marker and marital status are dealt with on the same footing as any other citizen's.
outOfScopeNotes:
The count for Rio Grande do Norte in 2025 is unresolved. One source reproducing the ANTRA 2025 dossier states zero registered trans killings in the state for 2025, while another reporting the same dossier's state ranking places Rio Grande do Norte at four, alongside Paraíba. The two figures have not been reconciled in the material held, and the per-capita rate of roughly 1.14 per million depends on which count is correct.

No Rio Grande do Norte statute, court decision or departmental instruction on the placement of LGBTI prisoners is sourced here. An overview of LGBT people in prison, read in full on 28 September 2026, contains no trans-prisoner housing rule for the state and reports only vulnerability and stigma effects, which is negative rather than affirmative evidence.

The prison-rights account relied on for social name, clothing choice and forwarding to women's prisons is footnoted to a media piece archived 18 January 2012, and its current legal status has not been verified against the text of Resolutions 348 and 366.

The population figure of approximately 3.5 million used for the per-capita calculation is an estimate carried in this record rather than a figure drawn from the cited sources. Both 2026 homicides are recent local press reports; arrest, charge and outcome in the Mossoró case, and the cause and perpetrator in the Praia da Pipa case, were not confirmed beyond the initial reporting.
